newsitem.title: CANADA: Manitoba declares emergency amid Red River flood.
newsitem.headline: Manitoba declares emergency amid Red River flood.

text.p: The Canadian province of Manitoba declared a state of emergency on Tuesday as more than 3,200 residents were ordered to flee their homes and 20,000 others were warned of possible evacuation orders in coming days.

"There is the potential for the entire valley to be evacuated and we are working with all the communities in the valley. There are close to 20,000 Manitobans living in the Red River Valley," provincial Premier Gary Filmon told reporters.

Police reported the first Canadian death linked to the flooding as four-year-old Kevin Michael Maendel of the New Rosedale Hutterite Colony near Portage-la-Prairie drowned in a culvert along the Assiniboine River, which drains into the Red.
Manitoba Government Services Minister Frank Pitura declared the provincial emergency from the U.S. border to the 51st Parallel, about 95 miles (152.9 km) north.
The declaration allows provincial officials to commandeer private property, put non-emergency workers to work on flood projects, ban travel and forcibly evacuate people.

Some 1.5 million sandbags were flown to Winnipeg on Tuesday by Canadian Armed Forces aircraft from Edmonton, Alberta. The city of Fargo, N.D. is trucking 75,000 bags to Winnipeg, about 60 miles (96.56 km) north of the U.S. border.
Winnipeg, the provincial capital, has more than 630,000 residents.

Floods in 1950 and 1979 left 400 square miles (1,036 sq km) of land between the U.S. border and Winnipeg under water. This year's flood may well cover double that area and take weeks to drain, emergency officials said.

"We haven't had a flood like this since the 1860s, so we're not sure how long the water will take to drain or when these people can return home," Manitoba Natural Resouces flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said.

Whitney said that while southern Manitoba communities were at high risk, a massive crescent-shaped ditch around Winnipeg should be able to divert the floodwaters. An estimate of the expected flood level was revised upward last Friday to 2 to 3 feet above the worst flood Manitoba has seen so far this century, Whitney said.

The town of Emerson, on the Canada-North Dakota border evacuated 750 residents, while 400 people abandoned their homes in Dominion City, 10 miles (16.09 km) north of the border and more than 1,000 residents of the town of Morris evacuated their homes, Pitura said.
Customs stations at Emerson and South Junction were closed on Tuesday ahead of Friday's forecast flood crest and 100 Canadian soldiers helped reinforce ring dikes at Emerson.
Meanwhile, 83 other people sought refuge behind ring dikes around St. Pierre Jolys as Red River tributaries overflowed, engulfing their homes, Clayton said.

"We're ready for the last record (flood) we had, but not for anything above that. We'll just have to do the best we can," said Morris Rural Municipality Reeve Herm Martens, the local equivalent of the mayor in Morris, 30 miles (48.28 km) south of Winnipeg..
Martens issued a voluntary evacuation order to more than 200 people in the district about 30 miles (48.28 km) north of the U.S. border.
Highway 75 to Winnipeg from the U.S. border was closed just south of the city late on Monday as other roads were washed out.
The Seine River began to overflow its banks on Tuesday afternoon and flooded town of Lorette 10 miles (16.09 kilometres) east of Winnipeg, Whitney said.
